terms.meaning: Only properties such as shape, size or state change, and no new substance forms.
One or more new substances form through a chemical reaction.
A substance reacts with oxygen and gives out heat, light or both.
The lowest temperature at which a substance catches fire.
Physical and chemical changes that slowly break rocks down, leading to soil.
Flowing water and wind carry soil and rock pieces away. It is a physical change.
Light made by a chemical change in a living thing, with no heat.

items.name: Lime water test
items.formula: Lime water + Carbon dioxide → Calcium carbonate + Water
items.example: Blow your breath into lime water through a straw and it turns milky.

items.name: Vinegar and baking soda
items.formula: Vinegar + Baking soda → Carbon dioxide + Other substances
items.example: The mixture fizzes, and the gas turns lime water milky.

items.name: Burning magnesium
items.formula: Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide + Heat + Light
items.example: A white powder is left behind.

items.name: Rusting as a chemical change
items.formula: Iron + moist air → rust, a new brown substance.
items.example: Rust is not iron any more, so a new substance has formed.

items.name: Fire triangle
items.formula: Fuel + Oxygen + Heat. Remove any one and the fire stops.
items.example: Water cools a fire below the ignition temperature of the fuel.

items.name: Candle under a tumbler
items.formula: The flame goes out when the oxygen inside is used up.
items.example: This shows that burning needs oxygen.

items.name: Clothes on fire
items.formula: Wrap the person in a thick woollen or cotton blanket to cut off the air.
items.example: Do not use synthetic cloth, because it melts and sticks to the skin.

items.name: Burning paper with a lens
items.formula: Focused sunlight heats paper up to its ignition temperature.
items.example: No flame touches the paper, yet it catches fire.

items.name: Burning candle
items.formula: Physical: wax melts and turns to vapour. Chemical: the wax vapour burns.
items.example: One process can have both kinds of change.

items.name: Fireflies
items.formula: A chemical change gives them light without heat.
items.example: This is why a firefly’s glow does not burn it.

items.name: Reversible changes
items.formula: The original can be brought back.
items.example: Melting ice, dissolving sugar, folding a handkerchief.

items.name: Irreversible changes
items.formula: The original cannot be brought back. This includes chemical changes and some physical ones.
items.example: Curdling milk and burning wood. Tearing paper too.

items.name: Desirable changes
items.example: Milk into curd, ripening fruit, waste into compost.

items.name: Undesirable changes
items.formula: Changes that we do not want.
items.example: Rusting, stored food going bad, and pollution from burning fuels.

items.name: Chemical weathering of rock
items.formula: Black basalt contains iron and slowly forms a red layer of iron oxide.
items.example: Water and air do this over a long time.

items.name: Physical weathering of rock
items.formula: Temperature changes, tree roots and freezing water crack rocks into smaller pieces.
items.example: Water that freezes in a crack pushes the rock apart.

mistakes.text: Not every physical change can be reversed. Torn paper is a physical change that cannot be undone.
Dissolving sugar in water is a physical change, because no new substance forms.
Weathering is both physical and chemical, but erosion is physical only.
Vinegar with common salt gives no carbon dioxide. Lime water stays clear, so do not expect fizzing with every mixture.
